subtopics.title: Evolution of the SDGs
subtopics.summary: The idea of sustainable development was defined in 1987 and then built into successive global commitments. Milestones such as the Millennium Development Goals, the Johannesburg Summit and Rio+20 moved the agenda forward. The 2015 adoption of the 2030 Agenda introduced 17 SDGs supported by 169 targets.
facts: 1987: Brundtland Commission defined the concept of sustainable development
1992: Earth Summit (UNCED) held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil
2000: Millennium Development Goals adopted, with 8 goals
2002: Johannesburg World Summit on Sustainable Development, also called Rio+10
2012: Rio+20 Conference laid the foundation for the SDGs
2015: 2030 Agenda and 17 SDGs adopted
The 2030 Agenda was adopted by all 193 UN Member States
17 Integrated Global Goals are supported by 169 Specific Targets
Objective: eliminate poverty, reduce inequality and protect the environment by 2030

subtopics.title: Earth Summit 1992 and its outcomes
subtopics.summary: The UN Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro, popularly called the Earth Summit, aimed to integrate environmental protection with sustainable development. Its key outcomes were the Rio Declaration, Agenda 21 and the Forest Principles. The Rio Declaration sets out guiding principles, Agenda 21 is a non-binding action plan, and the Forest Principles are non-legally binding.
facts: Popularly known as the Earth Summit (1992)
Objective: integrate environmental protection with sustainable development
Rio Declaration: a set of 27 Guiding Principles
Rio principles emphasise the precautionary approach and the polluter pays principle
Common but Differentiated Responsibilities is one of the Rio principles
Agenda 21: a non-binding action plan for sustainable development
Agenda 21 covers poverty, sustainable consumption and major groups
Forest Principles: non-legally binding principles on conservation and management of forests
Outcomes laid the foundation for the Kyoto Protocol (1997), Johannesburg Summit (2002) and Paris Agreement (2015)

subtopics.title: SDR 2026 findings and India's position
subtopics.summary: The 11th Sustainable Development Report 2026, released by the UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network, ranks countries on their SDG performance using a 0-100 score. India moved up to 94th place with an overall SDG Index score of 68.3 out of 100. Nearly half of all targets show only slow or limited progress, and the report identifies Zero Hunger as India's most critical development challenge.
facts: 11th Sustainable Development Report 2026, released by UN SDSN
Annual assessment of SDG progress, published since 2016
Assesses 193 UN Member States on a 0-100 SDG score
India ranked 94th, its highest position to date
India's overall SDG Index score: 68.3 out of 100
India improved from 112th position in 2015 to 94th in 2026
Approx 33.3% of India's SDG targets are expected to be achieved by 2030
Nearly half of all targets show only slow or limited progress
About 15% of targets have experienced setbacks compared with their 2015 baseline
Top performers: Finland, Sweden, Denmark; lowest: Chad, Central African Republic, South Sudan

subtopics.title: Climate finance
subtopics.summary: Climate finance refers to financing from public, private or alternative sources that supports mitigation and adaptation against climate change. It rests on the Polluter Pays principle and CBDR-RC, and multilateral climate funds are coordinated by the UNFCCC. Persistent challenges include gaps between national needs and funding, slow approvals and much lower per-capita approved funding for Least Developed Countries.
facts: Climate finance: local, national or transnational financing for climate action
Sources: public, private or alternative financing
Principles: Polluter Pays, and Common but Differentiated Responsibility and Respective Capability (CBDR-RC)
Multilateral climate funds are coordinated by the UNFCCC
Global Environment Facility (GEF): operating entity of the financial mechanism (1994)
Adaptation Fund gives developing countries full ownership of adaptation projects
Clean Development Mechanism: emission-reduction projects in developing nations
Green Climate Fund estd. 2010 (COP 16), with LDCF and SCCF under it
Loss and Damage Fund (2023): financial assistance to nations most affected by climate change
Challenges: slow rate of approvals and gaps between national needs and NDC finance

subtopics.title: Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0
subtopics.summary: The Panchayat Advancement Index 2.0 is a nationwide performance assessment framework for Gram Panchayats and Traditional Local Bodies. It grades local bodies from A+ to D on a composite score from 0 to 100. Tripura had the highest share of Front Runners, and no Gram Panchayat reached the Achiever grade.
facts: Nationwide performance assessment framework for Gram Panchayats and Traditional Local Bodies
Recognised as the first comprehensive index globally to evaluate rural local governance
Uses objective and verifiable indicators
Based on a composite score from 0 to 100
Achiever (A+) above 90; Front Runner (A) 75-89
Performer (B) 60-74; Aspirant (C) 40-59; Beginner (D) below 40
Translates 17 SDGs into 9 localised SDGs
Ministry of Panchayati Raj localises SDGs through this index
Top performers: Tripura (highest share of Front Runners), then Kerala and Odisha
No Gram Panchayat could reach the Achiever category

quizzes.passage:
The Sustainable Development Report is an annual assessment of how countries are progressing towards the Sustainable Development Goals. It gives each country a score on a scale of 0 to 100, which allows countries to be compared with one another. The report covers all UN Member States, and it is linked to the 2030 Agenda, the framework under which the goals were adopted. The goals cover a wide range of areas, including poverty, health, education and climate action.

The latest findings suggest that progress is uneven. A large share of targets is moving forward only slowly, while a smaller group of targets has slipped backwards compared with the position recorded in 2015. Some regions have improved more quickly than others, and the report draws attention to structural problems that affect particular goals.

India is one of the countries covered by the assessment. The report notes that its position has improved over time and that its overall performance has moved upward compared with earlier editions. Even so, only part of India's targets is expected to be achieved by 2030. Many of its targets are advancing at a pace that is insufficient to meet the deadline, and the report describes India's performance in terms of the goals where its progress is weakest.

Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals is tracked through an annual report, which has been published every year since 2016. The report scores each country on how close it is to achieving the goals, and it covers all UN Member States. Each goal is supported by specific targets, and a country's progress is judged by looking at those targets. The goals were adopted as part of the 2030 Agenda, which set a common deadline for the world to achieve them.

The latest edition finds that many goals are not on course for that deadline. A substantial share of targets is moving forward too slowly to be met in time, while a smaller group has slipped back compared with its starting point. Some regions have recorded rapid gains since 2015, and these gains stand out in the global picture.

India is among the countries assessed. Its position has improved over the years, and the report shows that the country has moved upward in the ranking. However, only part of its targets is expected to be reached on schedule. The report also examines the individual areas where the country's progress is weakest, and it identifies one goal as the most serious challenge for its development.

Climate finance refers to money that supports action against climate change, and it can come from local, national or transnational sources. Such action has two broad aims: reducing emissions, and helping communities adapt to the effects of climate change. Several multilateral funds have been set up to channel resources to these aims, and each fund has its own role and procedures. Their approaches differ, and some are designed around the needs of particular groups of countries. The arrangements include a number of different funds, each with its own structure, which is why the subject can seem complex.

Climate finance also rests on a set of principles that guide how responsibility is shared among countries. These principles reflect the fact that countries do not all contribute to the problem in the same way. Climate finance is discussed as part of the global response to climate change, and it is closely linked with the commitments that countries make in their national climate plans.

The system is not without difficulties. The funding that countries need for their climate plans does not always match what is available to them. The arrangements are still developing, and new funds continue to be considered as the global response evolves.

quizzes.passage:
Climate finance covers money that is spent on action against climate change, whether the funding comes from local, national or transnational sources. Such action has two main aims, namely reducing the emissions that cause warming and adapting to the changes that warming brings. A number of multilateral funds have been created to channel resources to these aims, and they operate under different arrangements. Some funds are linked to specific groups of countries. The arrangements are complex, and each fund works through its own rules for deciding which projects to support.

Climate finance is also guided by a set of principles about how responsibility should be shared between countries. These principles reflect the idea that countries have different levels of capability and different histories of contribution to the problem.

In practice, the system has faced difficulties. The funding that countries need under their own climate plans does not always match the money available to them. Projects can take a long time to be approved, and some groups of countries receive less approved funding in relation to their population than others. New funds continue to be set up to respond to particular needs, so the arrangements are still developing.

Gram Panchayats and other traditional local bodies form the base of rural governance, and a nationwide framework now assesses how these bodies perform. Each local body is evaluated and placed in a grade that reflects its standing against the framework's benchmarks. The framework relies on indicators that can be checked, so that the results rest on evidence rather than impressions.

The framework is also aligned with the global development agenda. It takes the broad global goals and turns them into a smaller set of goals that suit village-level planning. Thematic areas are part of the assessment as well, and these cover subjects such as livelihoods and health in rural communities. Results so far show that Tripura has the largest share of local bodies in the upper grades.

The grades form an ordered scale. They run from the highest tier, which is reserved for the strongest performance, down to the lowest tier. Each tier gives local bodies a clear reference point. The approach is nationwide, and it applies to Gram Panchayats across the country, which means that the same framework is used for bodies in every part of the country.

quizzes.passage:
Gram Panchayats and other traditional local bodies are the foundation of rural governance in India, and their performance is now assessed through a nationwide framework. The framework checks how well each body is doing in the areas that matter for local development, and it places each body in one of several grades. The assessment uses indicators that can be verified, which means that the results can be checked against evidence. Each local body receives a composite result based on these indicators, and that result determines its grade.

The grades run from the highest level to the lowest, which gives every body a clear benchmark. The framework is also tied to the Sustainable Development Goals, since it turns the global goals into a smaller set of goals suited to villages. Thematic areas form part of the assessment, covering themes such as livelihoods and healthy communities.

The framework is intended for Gram Panchayats and Traditional Local Bodies alike. Because it is nationwide, it applies across the country, and its grading scale gives local bodies in every state the same set of levels to aim for. Its purpose is to show where each body stands on the indicators it measures.
